claim: DNA polymerase I has long been viewed as the canonical model for DNA synthesis in cells.
source: DNA polymerase I (DNAP-I) has long been viewed as the canonical model for DNA synthesis in cells (Lehman et al., 1958).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lehman et al., 1958

claim: Structural insights into the mechanism of DNA synthesis have been obtained from crystal structures of a thermostable bacterial (Geobacillus stearothermophilus, Bst) DNAP-I large fragment that retains catalytic activity inside the crystal lattice.
source: Structural insights into the mechanism of DNA synthesis have been obtained from crystal structures of a thermostable bacterial (Geobacillus stearothermophilus, Bst) DNAP-I large fragment that retains catalytic activity inside the crystal lattice (Johnson et al., 2003; Kiefer et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to Johnson et al., 2003 and Kiefer et al., 1998

claim: The prevailing mechanism invokes the use of a distinct pre-insertion site, observed in the translocated product of in crystallo catalyzed primer-extension reactions where dNTP substrates are soaked into pre-formed crystals of DNAP-I bound to a primer-template duplex.
source: The prevailing mechanism invokes the use of a distinct pre-insertion site, observed in the translocated product of in crystallo catalyzed primer-extension reactions where dNTP substrates are soaked into pre-formed crystals of DNAP-I bound to a primer-template duplex (Figure 1—figure supplement 1)(Johnson et al., 2003; Kiefer et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to Johnson et al., 2003 and Kiefer et al., 1998, and reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: The pre-insertion site is a hydrophobic pocket located between the O and O1 helices of the finger subdomain where the n + 1 templating base resides prior to forming the nascent base pair with the incoming dNTP substrate.
source: The pre-insertion site is a hydrophobic pocket located between the O and O1 helices of the finger subdomain where the n + 1 templating base resides prior to forming the nascent base pair with the incoming dNTP substrate (Johnson et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Johnson et al., 2003

claim: The pre-insertion site has not been witnessed in polymerases with homologous active sites.
source: However, the pre-insertion site has not been witnessed in polymerases with homologous active sites (Eom et al., 1996; Li et al., 1998; Yin and Steitz, 2002), implying that DNAP-I follows a complex enzymatic pathway that contains numerous intermediates, many of which have not yet been observed in protein crystals.
evidence: Supported by citations to Eom et al., 1996; Li et al., 1998; Yin and Steitz, 2002

claim: DNAP-I follows a complex enzymatic pathway that contains numerous intermediates, many of which have not yet been observed in protein crystals.
source: However, the pre-insertion site has not been witnessed in polymerases with homologous active sites (Eom et al., 1996; Li et al., 1998; Yin and Steitz, 2002), implying that DNAP-I follows a complex enzymatic pathway that contains numerous intermediates, many of which have not yet been observed in protein crystals.
evidence: Inferred from the absence of pre-insertion site in homologous polymerases

claim: Five crystal structures of DNAP-I capture new conformations for the polymerase translocation and nucleotide pre-insertion steps in the DNA synthesis pathway.
source: Here we report five crystal structures of DNA polymerase I that capture new conformations for the polymerase translocation and nucleotide pre-insertion steps in the DNA synthesis pathway.
evidence: Reported as primary finding of the study

claim: In crystallo and solution catalyzed enzymatic reactions can produce different structural results with potentially different functional interpretations.
source: Recognizing that in crystallo and solution catalyzed enzymatic reactions can produce different structural results with potentially different functional interpretations (Ehrmann et al., 2017), we chose to investigate the translocated intermediates of DNAP-I using a direct crystallization method that involves solving crystal structures of the enzyme-product complex obtained from primer-extension reactions performed in solution rather than inside the environment of a protein crystal.
evidence: Supported by citation to Ehrmann et al., 2017

claim: The starting enzyme-primer-template complex was incubated with solutions of either buffer, dTTP, or dTTP and dATP for 30 min at 37°C.
source: In these reactions, the starting enzyme-primer-template complex was incubated with solutions of either buffer, dTTP, or dTTP and dATP for 30 min at 37°C.
evidence: Describes experimental procedure performed

claim: Cocrystal structures of Bst DNAP-I were solved to resolutions of 1.5 – 2.0 Å.
source: Following primer-extension, the enzyme-product complex was crystallized and cocrystal structures of Bst DNAP-I were solved to resolutions of 1.5 – 2.0 Å (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by data in Table 1

claim: High resolution structures of DNAP-I were obtained for the starting primer-template complex (n) and two translocated products obtained for the n + 1 and n + 2 nucleotide addition steps.
source: This approach was used to obtain high resolution structures of DNAP-I for the starting primer-template complex (n) and two translocated products obtained for the n + 1 and n + 2 nucleotide addition steps using the same primer-template duplex (n) described in previous in crystallo studies (Figure 1a)(Johnson et al., 2003).
evidence: Describes structures obtained in this study, with reference to Figure 1a and citation to Johnson et al., 2003

claim: Structures of the enzyme-primer-template complex (n) before catalysis reflect the initiation step of DNA synthesis.
source: Structures of the enzyme-primer-template complex (n) before catalysis reflect the initiation step of DNA synthesis.
evidence: Interpretation of structural data

claim: Superposition of the new structure obtained for the initiation step against the previously solved structure reveals that both structures adopt the same active site conformation.
source: Superposition of the new structure obtained for the initiation step against the previously solved structure reveals that both structures adopt the same active site conformation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: Supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2a

claim: Any structural differences observed between the translocated product of solution and in crystallo catalyzed reactions should be due to the catalysis environment rather than the starting polymerase conformation.
source: This result implies that any structural differences observed between the translocated product of solution and in crystallo catalyzed reactions should be due to the catalysis environment rather than the starting polymerase conformation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that starting structures are identical

claim: All of the structures adopt the same overall topology commonly observed for A-family DNA polymerases.
source: All of the structures adopt the same overall topology commonly observed for A-family DNA polymerases (Figure 1b).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figure 1b and established knowledge of A-family polymerases

claim: Careful analysis of the enzyme active site revealed clear conformational differences between structures obtained from solution-catalyzed reactions versus those obtained from in crystallo catalyzed reactions.
source: However, careful analysis of the enzyme active site did reveal clear conformational differences between structures obtained from solution-catalyzed reactions versus those obtained from in crystallo catalyzed reactions (Figure 1c,d).
evidence: Supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 1c,d

claim: The in crystallo catalyzed reactions adopt an active site conformation that is nearly identical to the starting conformation, which represents the initiation step of DNA synthesis.
source: The in crystallo catalyzed reactions adopt an active site conformation that is nearly identical to the starting conformation, which represents the initiation step of DNA synthesis (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: Supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2a

claim: The solution catalyzed reactions produce a different active site conformation that binds the duplex in a different position and base pair geometry.
source: However, the solution catalyzed reactions produce a different active site conformation that binds the duplex in a different position and base pair geometry (Figure 1—figure supplement 2b,c).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2b,c

claim: The solution catalyzed reactions produce a translocated product with markedly fewer contacts to the phosphodiester linkage, sugar, and nucleobase moieties of the primer-template duplex as compared to the translocated product obtained by in crystallo catalysis.
source: Major structural differences are depicted in the 2D interaction maps, which show that the solution catalyzed reactions produce a translocated product with markedly fewer contacts to the phosphodiester linkage, sugar, and nucleobase moieties of the primer-template duplex as compared to the translocated product obtained by in crystallo catalysis (Figure 1—figure supplements 3 and 4, Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: Supported by interaction maps shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 3 and 4, and Supplementary file 1a

claim: Tyr714 is a critical active site residue involved in the mechanism of DNA synthesis.
source: A particularly striking example of conformational disparity is Tyr714, a critical active site residue involved in the mechanism of DNA synthesis (Bell et al., 1997; Carroll et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bell et al., 1997 and Carroll et al., 1991

claim: In the solution catalyzed structures, Tyr714 stabilizes the newly formed base pair by stacking above the primer strand.
source: In the solution catalyzed structures, Tyr714 stabilizes the newly formed base pair by stacking above the primer strand, while this residue stacks above the template strand in the in crystallo catalyzed structures (Figure 1c,d).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figure 1c,d

claim: In the in crystallo catalyzed structures, Tyr714 stacks above the template strand.
source: In the solution catalyzed structures, Tyr714 stabilizes the newly formed base pair by stacking above the primer strand, while this residue stacks above the template strand in the in crystallo catalyzed structures (Figure 1c,d).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figure 1c,d

claim: The pre-insertion site is not observed in the solution catalyzed reactions due to a kink in the O-helix, which abrogates the O-O1 loop in the finger subdomain.
source: Importantly, the pre-insertion site is not observed in the solution catalyzed reactions due to a kink in the O-helix, which abrogates the O-O1 loop in the finger subdomain (Figure 1d).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figure 1d

claim: Absent a hydrophobic pocket, the n + 1 nucleotide in the template strand stacks against Tyr719 in the O1 helix, which positions the base for a subsequent round of catalysis.
source: Absent a hydrophobic pocket, the n + 1 nucleotide in the template strand stacks against Tyr719 in the O1 helix, which positions the base for a subsequent round of catalysis.
evidence: Interpretation of structural data

claim: The solution catalyzed structures obtained for the n + 1 and n + 2 translocated products adopt identical active site conformations.
source: The solution catalyzed structures obtained for the n + 1 and n + 2 translocated products adopt identical active site conformations (Figure 1 – figure supplement 2d), which together represent a new intermediate along the DNA replication pathway of Bst DNAP-I.
evidence: Supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 1 – figure supplement 2d

claim: The solution catalyzed structures represent a new intermediate along the DNA replication pathway of Bst DNAP-I.
source: The solution catalyzed structures obtained for the n + 1 and n + 2 translocated products adopt identical active site conformations (Figure 1 – figure supplement 2d), which together represent a new intermediate along the DNA replication pathway of Bst DNAP-I.
evidence: Interpretation of structural data shown in Figure 1 – figure supplement 2d

claim: dATP was soaked into a crystal of the n + 1 translocated product obtained by crystallization of a solution catalyzed reaction.
source: Accordingly, dATP was soaked into a crystal of the n + 1 translocated product obtained by crystallization of a solution catalyzed reaction.
evidence: Describes experimental procedure performed

claim: Following one cycle of in crystallo catalysis, an n + 2 translocated structure was produced that contained the pre-insertion site and matched the active site conformation of previous in crystallo results.
source: Following one cycle of in crystallo catalysis, an n + 2 translocated structure was produced that now contained the pre-insertion site and matched the active site conformation of previous in crystallo results (Figure 1 – figure supplement 2e, f).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figure 1 – figure supplement 2e, f

claim: In crystallo catalysis favors an active site conformation that contains the pre-insertion site, as the same active site conformation is obtained from two different starting points.
source: This observation demonstrates that in crystallo catalysis favors an active site conformation that contains the pre-insertion site, as the same active site conformation is obtained from two different starting points.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that different starting conformations converge to the same in crystallo conformation

claim: The translocated product obtained from the set of solution catalyzed reactions is similar to known Bst DNAP-I structures solved with duplexes that contain damaged DNA intermediates and active site mutations.
source: Interestingly, the translocated product obtained from the set of solution catalyzed reactions is similar to known Bst DNAP-I structures solved with duplexes that contain damaged DNA intermediates and active site mutations (Figure 1—figure supplement 5, Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: Supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5 and Supplementary file 1b

claim: Structures with damaged DNA intermediates and active site mutations were previously thought to contain a distorted active site conformation due to the position of Tyr714 relative to its conformation in the in crystallo catalysis structures.
source: These structures were previously thought to contain a distorted active site conformation due to the position of Tyr714 relative to its conformation in the in crystallo catalysis structures (Gehrke et al., 2013; Johnson and Beese, 2004; Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gehrke et al., 2013; Johnson and Beese, 2004; Wang et al., 2012

claim: Tyr714 functions as a regulatory checkpoint in the mechanism of DNA synthesis by evaluating the geometry of the newly formed base pair.
source: However, given the homology of these structures to the translocated product of solution catalyzed reactions, we postulate that Tyr714 functions as a regulatory checkpoint in the mechanism of DNA synthesis by evaluating the geometry of the newly formed base pair.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on structural homology

claim: Wu and colleagues solved the ternary structure of a mutant version of Bst DNAP-I bound to an incoming dATP substrate.
source: Previously, Wu and colleagues solved the ternary structure of a mutant version of Bst DNAP-I bound to an incoming dATP substrate (Miller et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Miller et al., 2015

claim: The structure by Wu and colleagues was originally described as an open ternary complex.
source: Although that structure was originally described as an open ternary complex, presumably to avoid confusion with the pre-insertion site, it resembles the pre-insertion complex first observed in Klentaq1 (Li et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 1998

claim: The key difference between the open ternary and pre-insertion complex is whether the incoming nucleotide is paired opposite the templating base or an active site residue.
source: The key difference between the open ternary and pre-insertion complex is whether the incoming nucleotide is paired opposite the templating base or an active site residue (Doublié et al., 1998; Yin and Steitz, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Doublié et al., 1998 and Yin and Steitz, 2004

claim: The structure by Wu and colleagues shows the incoming substrate paired opposite Tyr714, and should be considered a pre-insertion complex.
source: Since the structure by Wu and colleagues shows the incoming substrate paired opposite Tyr714, it should be considered a pre-insertion complex.
evidence: Inference based on structural features and definition of pre-insertion complex

claim: The wild-type polymerase is capable of forming a pre-insertion complex.
source: We demonstrated that the wild-type polymerase is also capable of forming a pre-insertion complex by solving the ternary structure of the enzyme bound to the non-hydrolyzable analog, dAMPNPP.
evidence: Demonstrated by solving a new crystal structure

claim: The ternary structure of wild-type Bst DNAP-I bound to dAMPNPP closely resembles the mutant Bst polymerase structure determined by Wu and colleagues and shows Tyr714 paired opposite the incoming nucleotide.
source: The resulting structure (Figure 2) closely resembles the mutant Bst polymerase structure determined by Wu and colleagues and shows Tyr714 paired opposite the incoming nucleotide (Miller et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figure 2 and citation to Miller et al., 2015

claim: The phosphate tail of dAMPNPP shows nearly 100% occupancy.
source: Although the phosphate tail shows nearly 100% occupancy, the sugar and nucleobase moieties are flexible, which is consistent with the dynamic properties of the incoming nucleotide in an open polymerase conformation.
evidence: Observation from structural data

claim: The sugar and nucleobase moieties of dAMPNPP are flexible, which is consistent with the dynamic properties of the incoming nucleotide in an open polymerase conformation.
source: Although the phosphate tail shows nearly 100% occupancy, the sugar and nucleobase moieties are flexible, which is consistent with the dynamic properties of the incoming nucleotide in an open polymerase conformation.
evidence: Interpretation of structural data based on established knowledge

claim: The incoming nucleotide is stabilized by polar contacts to the negatively charged triphosphate moiety.
source: Nevertheless, the structure shows that the incoming nucleotide is stabilized by polar contacts to the negatively charged triphosphate moiety.
evidence: Observation from structural data

claim: Bst DNAP-I adopts a pre-insertion complex similar to other A-family DNA polymerases.
source: These observations demonstrate that Bst DNAP-I adopts a pre-insertion complex similar to other A-family DNA polymerases (Rothwell and Waksman, 2005), which clarifies an important step in the mechanism of DNA synthesis.
evidence: Supported by structural data and citation to Rothwell and Waksman, 2005

claim: The catalytic cycle of DNAP-I consists of four key steps that derive from high resolution structures of Bst DNAP-I and its homolog T7 RNA polymerase.
source: Based on the structures reported here, we propose a revised mechanism for DNA synthesis by DNA polymerase I. The catalytic cycle consists of four key steps that derive from high resolution structures of Bst DNAP-I and its homolog T7 RNA polymerase (Figure 3).
evidence: Proposed mechanism based on structural data shown in Figure 3

claim: Starting from the newly determined post-translocation complex, the polymerase undergoes a conformation change to adopt the pre-insertion complex with an incoming nucleotide paired opposite Tyr714 in the enzyme active site.
source: Starting from the newly determined post-translocation complex, the polymerase undergoes a conformation change to adopt the pre-insertion complex with an incoming nucleotide paired opposite Tyr714 in the enzyme active site.
evidence: Proposed mechanism based on structural data

claim: The conformational change from post-translocation to pre-insertion complex involves release of the n + 1 templating base from its stacking interaction with Tyr719 in the O1 helix and the repositioning of Tyr714 in the enzyme active site.
source: This conformational change involves release of the n + 1 templating base from its stacking interaction with Tyr719 in the O1 helix and the repositioning of Tyr714 in the enzyme active site.
evidence: Proposed mechanism based on structural data

claim: The enzyme undergoes a more significant conformational change to adopt the closed ternary complex, which defines the pre-catalytic state of the enzyme.
source: The enzyme then undergoes a more significant conformational change to adopt the closed ternary complex (Johnson et al., 2003), which defines the pre-catalytic state of the enzyme.
evidence: Proposed mechanism based on structural data and citation to Johnson et al., 2003

claim: Immediately following phosphodiester bond formation, the enzyme adopts a post-catalytic complex in which the primer has been extended by one nucleotide.
source: Immediately following phosphodiester bond formation, the enzyme adopts a post-catalytic complex in which the primer has been extended by one nucleotide (Yin and Steitz, 2004).
evidence: Proposed mechanism based on citation to Yin and Steitz, 2004

claim: The enzyme translocates to the next position on the template to initiate another cycle of nucleotide addition.
source: The enzyme then translocates to the next position on the template to initiate another cycle of nucleotide addition.
evidence: Proposed mechanism based on established knowledge of polymerase function

claim: The new structures, along with previously solved structures obtained by in crystallo catalysis, highlight the dynamic nature of the finger subdomain in the enzyme active site.
source: We suggest that these new structures, along with previously solved structures obtained by in crystallo catalysis, highlight the dynamic nature of the finger subdomain in the enzyme active site.
evidence: Interpretation of structural data

claim: The new and existing structures expand our understanding of the mechanism of DNA synthesis by capturing important intermediates in a complicated reaction pathway.
source: Together, the new and existing structures expand our understanding of the mechanism of DNA synthesis by capturing important intermediates in a complicated reaction pathway.
evidence: Summary interpretation of the study's findings

claim: The translocation complex is stabilized by π-stacking interactions between Tyr719 and the n + 1 templating base and between Tyr714 and the primer strand.
source: The translocation complex (top) is stabilized by π-stacking interactions between Tyr719 and the n + 1 templating base and between Tyr714 and the primer strand.
evidence: Description of structural features shown in Figure 3

claim: In the translocation complex, Tyr714 occupies the insertion site (IS) while a newly formed base pair is located in the post insertion site (post-IS).
source: Tyr714 occupies the insertion site (IS, purple) while a newly formed base pair is located in the post insertion site (post-IS, green).
evidence: Description of structural features shown in Figure 3

claim: In the pre-insertion complex, the O-helix adjusts to accommodate the incoming dNTP substrate, which binds opposite Tyr714 in the IS.
source: In the pre-insertion complex (right), the O-helix adjusts to accommodate the incoming dNTP substrate, which binds opposite Tyr714 in the IS.
evidence: Description of structural features shown in Figure 3

claim: In the closed ternary complex, the polymerase undergoes a major conformational change to allow the n + 1 templating base to form a nascent base pair with the dNTP substrate in pre-catalytic state.
source: In the closed ternary complex (bottom), the polymerase undergoes a major conformational change to allow the n + 1 templating base to form a nascent base pair with the dNTP substrate in pre-catalytic state.
evidence: Description of structural features shown in Figure 3

claim: Following catalysis, the finger subdomain remains closed with a trapped pyrophosphate moiety observed in the active site of the post-catalytic complex.
source: Following catalysis, the finger subdomain remains closed with a trapped pyrophosphate moiety observed in the active site of the post-catalytic complex (left).
evidence: Description of structural features shown in Figure 3

claim: To complete the cycle, the finger subdomain opens, pyrophosphate is released, and the enzyme translocates to the next position on the template.
source: To complete the cycle, the finger subdomain opens, pyrophosphate is released, and the enzyme translocates to the next position on the template.
evidence: Proposed mechanism based on established knowledge

claim: The translocation, pre-insertion, and closed ternary complexes are based on crystal structures of Bst DNAP-I.
source: The translocation (6DSY), pre-insertion (6DSU), and closed ternary complexes (1VL5) are based on crystal structures Bst DNAP-I.
evidence: Specifies the structural basis for the proposed mechanism

claim: The post-catalytic complex is based on the structure of T7 RNAP, which is a homolog of Bst DNAP-I.
source: The post-catalytic complex is based on the structure of T7 RNAP (1S77), which is a homolog of Bst DNAP-I.
evidence: Specifies the structural basis for the proposed mechanism
